title: Chicken breast, fried, coated, skin/coating eaten, from raw

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is a lean cut of poultry meat, rich in protein. When deep‑fried or pan‑fried in a coating it develops a crispy golden crust that is eaten together with the meat. This product is common in fast‑food, snack items and quick‑cook dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast provides about 31 g of protein per 100 g, making it an excellent protein source.
Frying in a coating roughly doubles the calorie content compared with raw breast.
Traditional breading in many countries often uses breadcrumbs, flour and spices.
Poultry is considered “white” meat and is generally easier to digest than red meat.
Proper frying retains some B‑vitamins, though a portion is lost due to high heat.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: The protein in chicken breast contains all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat in raw form
items.content: Raw breast meat is very low in fat, making it a good base for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B3 (niacin) and B6 (pyridoxine) support energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Chicken breast supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The high protein content helps maintain a feeling of fullness, useful for weight management.

items.title: High calorie after frying
items.content: The coating and oil significantly increase the product’s energy density, which can contribute to weight gain if consumed frequently.

items.title: Presence of trans fats
items.content: Frying in certain oils can generate trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked chicken may contain Salmonella or Campylobacter; it should be cooked to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Chicken meat allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Coated fried chicken breast is convenient as a hot snack, added to salads, sandwiches, or served with dipping sauces. Let it rest a few minutes after cooking to keep the crust crisp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw breast in the refrigerator at + 2‑4 °C for up to 2 days or freeze. Cooked fried coated pieces should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge for no more than 3 days; for longer storage freeze, though the crust may lose some crispness.
